newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi's Buyoya calls national debate on future.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya calls national debate on future.

text.p: Burundian President Pierre Buyoya on Friday called a national debate to start on January 28 to try to end civil war in the tiny central African country.
Buyoya, who came to power in a July 25 coup, told a news conference that not all Burundians held similar views on how to end fighting and he wanted to listen to the opinion of everyone.
But Buyoya said views of radical armed opposition groups, such as Hutu rebels of the militant CNDD party, would not be welcome until the rebels rejected the use of force.

"The national debate is intended to search for a way to end the war. We wish to get all Burundians together to study the issue, as well as other important issues in the life and future of our country," Buyoya told reporters in Bujumbura.

Asked by reporters whether he wanted the national debate to mandate him to talk to armed rebels, Buyoya said: "I have always said that my government was ready to talk to them. The only condition remains their abandoning armed opposition."
Buyoya lamented that since he restored the national assembly late last year, parliament had not made any contribution to the development of the country.

Many parliament members, ethnic Hutus, are in exile. They fear they could be killed in a country where ethnic strife between majority Hutus and the minority Tutsi has killed more than 150,000 people since low-intensity war began in 1993.
The civil war was ignited by the killing of Hutu elected president Melchior Ndadaye by Tutsi soldiers.
Buyoya, a moderate Tutsi, toppled Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya in the July 25 bloodless uprising.

Buyoya said his government had moved to stem indiscipline in the Tutsi-dominated army and in recent days eight soldiers had been arrested in in connection with civilian killings. He suggested that up to 500 soldiers had been arrested in Burundi since the coup.
A Burundi army spokesman told Reuters last week that soldiers shot dead 126 Burundian Hutu refugees who had been expelled from Tanzania and tried to escape from a detention centre in Burundi.

These killings in the ethnically-divided central African nation came a day after witnesses and other sources accused the army of massacring at least 83 civilians in a single operation last Sunday night.
Burundi is at war between the army and Hutu rebels fighting for a greater political stake in the tiny tea and coffee-growing country whose government and army are dominated by the Tutsi.
